A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MotionGPT3. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support matching corresponding content despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original HumanML3D generation, captioning, reconstruction, retrieval and ablation results, including extensive appendix experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original HumanML3D experiments, including revised generation and captioning results, component controls and appendix ablations.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the continuous motion VAE, separate text and motion branches with shared attention, diffusion head, and three-stage training procedure. v1 Appendix D already describes attention-based conditioning and motion-boundary handling elaborated in v2. Expanded implementation descriptions and renamed interfaces do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: HumanML3D generation, captioning, reconstruction and the four TMR retrieval scenarios remain. However, v2 removes the explicit non-motion weather-question demonstration in v1 Figure 2, modestly narrowing the demonstrated scenarios. No new motion dataset is reported.

E2.justification: v2 adds MotionDiffuse to the generation comparison in Appendix Table 6 and MotionGPT-2 and MG-MotionLLM to the unified-model comparison in Figure 8. TM2T also joins the qualitative captioning comparison in Figure 6. Most existing benchmark comparators remain, sometimes relocated.

E3.justification: Single-task generation training changes from 100 epochs in v1 Table 1 to 200 in v2. Section 4.1 reverses the reported backbone/head learning rates, from 2e-4/1e-4 to 1e-4/2e-4. Joint fine-tuning changes from 140k iterations in v1 Appendix C.5 to 50k in v2 Section 4.4. These substantially revise reported settings without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a single-stream-plus-VQ control in Table 3 and a matched-loss checkpoint analysis in Figure 3. Captioning case studies are replaced, while the zero-initialized CFG control and guidance settings 7, 8 and 9 disappear. Most scaling, attention, diffusion-head and training-stage analyses already existed in v1's appendix.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 11-13 newly specify averaging the head, guidance and training-stage ablations over two runs. This is newly disclosed run information, not evidence of increased replication. Both versions already specify 20 generation evaluations with 95% confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Results change substantially across benchmark and ablation tables. For example, the unified model's generation FID changes from 0.155 to 0.208 and captioning BLEU@4 from 9.793 to 19.412. TMR All text-to-motion R@1 changes from 10.01 to 9.60, and attention and training-stage results are revised. Changed training settings prevent interpreting these replacements as controlled performance gains.

T1.justification: The diffusion formulation and noise-prediction objective remain unchanged. v2 Appendix D explicitly writes standard VAE, KL and evaluation formulas for components already used in v1; these provide additional explanation rather than new theoretical assumptions, results, proofs or substantive derivations.

C1.justification: The central continuous-latent, bimodal-model contribution remains. v2 drops v1's introductory state-of-the-art claim for motion prediction and reduces the headline emphasis on preserving general language intelligence. It specifies approximately 2x training-loss and up to 4x validation convergence speedups, refining the earlier efficiency claim.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the broad human-body-only limitation with specific directional-control failures, single-latent restrictions on long-motion composition, and limited out-of-domain generalization. It also expands the interpretation of evaluator saturation into possible embedding-space overfitting and describes final-stage tuning as modest refinement. The principal quantization and cross-modal-interference explanations remain.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: VAE training uses batch size 256 for 150k iterations, default holder count and CFG scale are specified, and Appendix D details hidden-state dimensions, pooling, residual-block operations, VAE losses and the 263-dimensional motion representation. Evaluation and qualitative-rendering procedures are also documented more explicitly. These disclosures mostly clarify existing components.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially broaden positioning around multimodal adapters, frozen language models and multi-objective optimization. Added discussions include Flamingo, BLIP-2, NExT-GPT, conflict-averse optimization and gradient surgery. This extends the scientific rationale beyond v1's shorter unified-model and mixture-of-experts discussion, rather than merely updating citation formatting.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Training-efficiency analysis moves into the main narrative, benchmark comparisons and component ablations are separated, and appendix sections are reordered and subdivided. Terminology, citation style and conference headers also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws architecture diagrams, moves and annotates training curves, reorganizes single-task and unified comparison tables, and replaces captioning illustrations. Existing capacity and attention-depth tables are partly converted into plots, and attention-connection schematics are added. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

improvement.justification: Clearer experimental organization, added controls, fuller implementation information and more concrete limitations modestly improve assessability and reproducibility. Much supporting evidence already existed in v1, and unreconciled revisions limit the gain: v2 Appendix C.6 still quotes the earlier catastrophic-forgetting BERTScore of 0.713, although its revised Table 13 reports 33.385. The revision improves documentation overall but does not fully reconcile its interpretations with the updated evidence.
